source.title: Scaling Language-Free Visual Representation Learning
source.authors: David Fan; Shengbang Tong; Jia-Cheng Zhu; Koustuv Sinha; Zhuang Liu; Xinlei Chen; Michael G. Rabbat; Nicolas Ballas; Yann LeCun; Amir Bar; Sai-Ning Xie

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; some figures and tables are flattened or garbled.
record.tranche_reason: Extends visual representation scaling to web-scale self-supervised image models and reports downstream VQA performance as model size and training examples increase.
record.gate_note: The study measures visual-encoder downstream VQA accuracy, not language-model held-out cross-entropy or fitted loss power laws. It does not test compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. VQA score values in the scaling figures are figure-only, so no values have been inferred from the plots.
record.test_reason: The study trains vision encoders (Web-DINO 1B–7B, Web-MAE 1B–5B, CLIP 1B–7B) on MC-2B and on ImageNet-1k. It reports downstream VQA accuracy, measured through a frozen encoder plus Llama-3 8B, as model size and images seen grow. This bears on V6 in a new setting: vision encoders rather than language models. It reports no pretraining loss, fits no power law and makes no forecast, so V1–V5 and V7 are untested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but it misses the main claim. Trained on the same MC-2B data as CLIP, visual SSL scales better than CLIP with model size and data. It does not saturate up to 7B and reaches CLIP-level VQA. Gains depend on data: no scaling on ImageNet-1k, and text-rich filtering boosts OCR & Chart. The authors fit no scaling laws.
record.recipe_differences: The study scales visual self-supervised image encoders and measures downstream VQA accuracy; it does not measure held-out language-model cross-entropy or fit the original language-model scaling-law method.
record.method_sensitivity: Observed scaling depends on pretraining data: MC-2B models improve with size, while ImageNet-1k models show no clear scaling trend. VQA categories also differ: General and Knowledge saturate at some data amounts, Vision-Centric gains level off beyond 2B examples, and OCR & Chart continues improving.
record.code_released: not stated; the authors say they plan to open-source the Web-SSL vision models
record.peer_reviewed: IEEE International Conference on Computer Vision (ICCV), 2025
record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported for the scaling results. The plotted scaling values are not numerically recoverable from the supplied text; conclusions are presented as trends rather than fitted predictive laws.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted due to the 60-row limit. Classic-vision benchmark scaling results are not separately cataloged here; the extracted rows focus on VQA outcomes relevant to the downstream-performance version.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss is reported, and no power law in parameters, data or compute is fitted.
There is no extrapolation from small runs.
There is no compute-optimal allocation analysis.
Architecture shapes (Table 1) vary with size and are not compared at a fixed parameter count.
The study is in the image modality, but it reports no loss and fits no power law, so whether the same law form holds is not tested.

Vision encoders are not language models. The study makes no prediction from pretraining loss, fits no scaling law and makes no forecast. Only the monotonic improvement of downstream VQA with size and data is tested.
No fitting choices or exponents are compared.

missing.what: Classic vision scaling. IN1k linear rises 84.70→86.00 with size. ADE20K linear is non-monotonic (46.60, 50.55, 50.17, 49.54, 49.08). NYUd error worsens at 5B/7B. With more data at 7B, ADE20K linear falls 49.08→42.14 and NYUd lin.1 error rises 0.380→0.491.
Category-level data scaling: General and Knowledge VQA saturate at 4B and 2B images, Vision-Centric saturates after 2B, OCR & Chart keeps improving.
All per-size average VQA values are given numerically in the appendix tables. The rows wrongly mark them as figure-only.

record.verdict_notes: The V6 link is a T3 stretch: the systems are vision encoders evaluated through a fixed Llama-3 8B MLLM, not language models, and the paper describes trends, not predictive laws. No uncertainty is reported, and VQA differences of around one point may be noise. The architecture changes across sizes (the 1B model is deeper and narrower), which confounds the size sweep.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out language-model loss is measured, and no loss scaling law is fitted.
No small-run fit is used to predict larger-run loss.
No fixed-compute parameter/token allocation is studied.
No controlled comparison isolates depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The study scales image encoders, but it does not test whether a power law in held-out pretraining loss holds in another modality or training regime.
The study reports downstream visual VQA trends with scale, but does not test prediction from pretraining loss or make forecasts from smaller runs.
No fitting choices or scaling-law exponents are compared.

relationships.condition: Web-DINO (1B–7B) and Web-MAE (1B–5B) pretrained on MC-2B with 2B images seen; average VQA
relationships.reason: Average VQA rises monotonically with size: Web-DINO 49.01→53.87, Web-MAE 49.19→51.50 (Tables 6, 11).
relationships.display_finding: Average VQA increased monotonically from 49.01 to 53.87 for Web-DINO and from 49.19 to 51.50 for Web-MAE.

relationships.condition: Web-DINO ViT-7B, 1B→8B MC-2B images seen; average VQA
relationships.reason: Average VQA goes 51.02→53.87→54.37→55.24 with diminishing increments (Table 8).
relationships.display_finding: Average VQA increased from 51.02 through 53.87 and 54.37 to 55.24, with diminishing increments.

relationships.reason: Average VQA gains under 1 point up to 3B, then falls slightly at 5B and 7B (52.30–53.22, Table 12).
relationships.display_finding: Average VQA improved by less than one point through 3B, then declined slightly at 5B and 7B, within a 52.30–53.22 range.

relationships.reason: Average VQA stays flat at 45.99–46.43 across sizes (Table 10). Scaling the model gives nothing when data is small or narrow.
relationships.display_finding: Average VQA remained nearly flat at 45.99–46.43 across model sizes.

relationships.condition: Classic vision tasks and individual VQA categories (text-based; no rows)
relationships.reason: Tables 7 and 9: IN1k gains are modest, while ADE20K linear and NYU depth get worse with size and with more data. Several VQA categories saturate (Section 3.2).
relationships.display_finding: ImageNet-1k gains were modest, ADE20K linear segmentation and NYU depth worsened with larger models and more data, and several VQA categories saturated.
